messages.subject: second question
parts:
Now I have a new problem - I am exploring the relationship between a drug concentration and an enzyme activity.  I have time-concentration data, and time-effect data (in terms of enzyme activity)
ID TIME CONC EFFECT
1 0 0 425
1 1 200
1 5
50
1 10 50 300
2 0 0 400
2 1 300 45
2 5 200
2 10 100 200
I would like to co-plot time and conc and effect on the same graph.  
The following code
PKPD <- merge(DPP4, sita, by =c("ID","TIME"), all=TRUE)
PKPD<-as.data.frame(PKPD)
PKPD <-melt(PKPD, id=c("ID","TIME"))
p<-ggplot(PKPD, aes(x=TIME, y=value, colour=variable))
p+geom_point()+facet_wrap (~ID)+scale_y_log10(breaks=c(0,1,10,100), labels=c(0,1,10,100))

allows me look at scatter plots of both variables by colour, but I really would like to join the points with a smooth line (even though the data is at times missing), just so I can explore the relationship visually

if I insert + geom_line() it get lines between continuous data, but breaks for the discontinous data - ideally, I just want smooth lines between the available point

thanks for any help

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: second question
parts:
Firstly, thank you for the combination of data and code (although I had to manually insert NAs in place of the blanks so that R could read it...but I digress).

I don't see any option to apply a custom NA action to geom_line(). geom_line() is doing what it says it does: "Connect observations, in ordered (sic) by x value". Let's consider CONC vs TIME on ID1. It draws a line from (0, 0) to (1, 200), then from TIME = 1 to TIME = 5, it connects 200 and NA. As expected, nothing is drawn. Ditto for connecting (5, NA) to (10, 50). 

The way to get rid of the problem is to get rid of the NAs after the data are melted (because then the CONC and EFFECT values are disaggregated). Here's your toy example in this context:

# library('ggplot2')

# To keep Brandon happy, the output from dput() ;)
# RHS is the return from dput(d), where d is the name
# of the input data frame
d <- structure(list(ID = c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L), TIME = c(0L,
1L, 5L, 10L, 0L, 1L, 5L, 10L), CONC = c(0L, 200L, NA, 50L, 0L,
300L, 200L, 100L), EFFECT = c(425L, NA, 50L, 300L, 400L, 45L,
NA, 200L)), .Names = c("ID", "TIME", "CONC", "EFFECT"), class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA,
-8L))

# Melt the data:
dm <- melt(d, id = c('ID', 'TIME'))

# Initial plot:
ggplot(dm, aes(x = TIME, y = value, colour = variable)) +
    geom_line(size = 1) + facet_wrap(~ ID)

# Remove the NAs from the responses:
dm2 <- dm[!is.na(value), ]

# Replot:
ggplot(dm2, aes(x = TIME, y = value, colour = variable)) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    geom_line(size = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~ ID)

I suggest plotting both the points and lines so that it is clear where the missing data lie.

I may tease Brandon about dput(), but he's absolutely right. dput() has many advantages, the two most important of which are: (i) it is a text representation of the (data) object and hence safe to copy and paste into an e-mail, and more importantly, (ii) it retains the class structure of your (data) object as it exists on your machine - i.e., there is no information loss in translation, unlike the case when people copy and paste data snippets into an e-mail. A third reason is that it isn't hard to generate: dput(object).  The other safe alternative is to provide the code to generate the data object, which is common when people supply fake data.

HTH,
Dennis
